data.title: Pentagon has no department-wide plan to address munitions shortages, watchdog report finds
data.description:
Despite a munitions shortfall exacerbated by the Trump administration’s war in Iran, the Pentagon does not have a department-wide plan to address the issue long-term, a federal watchdog said in a new report released Thursday.

The Government Accountability Office found that while the Defense Department has taken steps toward increasing its munitions inventory, it “doesn’t have an overarching plan that identifies long-term goals, strategies, or ways to measure its progress.”

As part of the problem, the Pentagon does not have a dedicated office with authority to improve munition inventories, making it harder for the department “to know whether its munitions production efforts are really addressing department-wide needs.”

The status of U.S. munitions reserves remains murky at best, but what is known is that Washington blew through a significant portion of its long-range cruise missiles and interceptors in the beginning of the Iran war, which began on Feb. 28.

In March, for example, it was reported that U.S. forces burned through at least 850 Tomahawk missiles in the first month of the conflict known as Operation Epic Fury. It’s estimated the Pentagon has just a few thousand left.

And in August, Reuters reported the Army had used up “virtually all” of its global stockpile of long-range missiles such as ATACMS and Precision Strike Missiles.

While top administration officials have insisted the U.S. military has the weapons needed for an intense military offensive against Iran should fighting resume, Acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao on Tuesday revealed this week that his service recoded and fired missiles he described as “expired.”

“A lot of the munitions we used in Epic Fury, we were able to recode those,” Cao said during a Senate Armed Services Committee hearing on his nomination to become Navy secretary. 

“They were code echo, code foxtrot, which means they’re expired. But, you know, I came from a poor family, right? Things like bread doesn’t expire. You just rub some water on it, microwave it for 15 seconds and it’s good to go,” he said.

Reports also have suggested that weapons shortages are a factor in persuading President Trump to hold back on escalating attacks against Iran.

“A key part of military readiness is having a reliable supply of munitions, including bombs, missiles, and torpedoes. But the Department of Defense has faced persistent munitions shortages,” the GAO wrote in a summary of its new report. “The 2026 conflict with Iran only reinforced the challenges with the munitions inventory.”

“DOD has taken steps toward increasing its inventory, but could do more,” the watchdog adds, noting that in lieu of a plan, the Pentagon and the military services “can be reactive to global events rather than driven by total requirements.”

And while DOD has a department-wide munitions data tool to track munitions, the GAO found that it has limited oversight over this instrument has not regularly conducted inventory check ins with the services.

The watchdog recommended that the Pentagon come up with an overarching plan to improve inventory levels that links building munitions and funding to department requirements and include long-term goals, strategies to achieve them and ways to gauge progress.

In addition, it suggests the Defense secretary identify an office to implement the munitions plan and set regular timelines to check munitions inventories.

The Hill reached out to the Pentagon for comment on the report.

data.title: Trump brushes off Musk distancing from MAGA
data.description:
President Trump brushed off comments from tech titan Elon Musk that he isn’t part of Trump’s “Make America Great Again” (MAGA) movement, and that he felt “pretty foolish” for the hundreds of millions of dollars he spent backing Republicans in the midterms.

“He’s a friend of mine,” Trump told NBC News in a phone call Thursday while flying back from Asia.  “What can I tell you? I mean, you have to ask — there are lots of definitions out there.”

“MAGA, to me, means something very specific, and when people veer from it, they don’t do very well,” he continued. “But Elon is — Elon’s got very good intentions. I mean, he was with me the whole — he traveled with me.”

Musk, speaking remotely to The New York Times’s Andrew Ross Sorkin at the annual DealBook summit Wednesday, said that he is “not MAGA.”

He added, “at least I’m not like — I’m not sure what MAGA means, but I don’t think I’m like, if that means sort of blind adherence to a set of policies by the Republican Party, then I certainly don’t have that.”

“I think there are positives and negatives in both parties,” he said.

The Tesla and Space X CEO spent a whopping $442 million on Republican campaigns for this year’s midterms. Ultimately, Democrats won both the House and the Senate.

“I feel pretty foolish about having spent so much money and not seeing much for it,” Musk said. “Or maybe it would’ve been much worse without that. But it certainly shows that American elections are not just about money. Obviously, you can put a lot of money into an election and have an effect that is relatively minor, and I think that was the case here.”

Trump and Musk have had a very public on-again, off-again relationship.

Musk had a history of criticizing Trump, but then backed him during the 2024 presidential campaign, pumping nearly $300 million in Trump’s and other Republicans’ campaigns.

Trump put him in charge of the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), a new office created by the administration to cut government spending.

The tech billionaire left DOGE in 2025, and the two had a brief falling out, but have since become closer again. He traveled with Trump for the president’s trip this week to China for the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation.

data.title: UN court rules that Myanmar committed genocide against Rohingya
data.description:
The United Nations’s International Court of Justice (ICJ) on Thursday found in a new ruling that Myanmar committed genocide against its Rohingya Muslim population, following thousands of deaths amid the county’s “clearance operations” in 2017.

The Hague-based world court said Myanmar violated its obligation to prevent the destruction of evidence in connection with allegations of genocide, and that it violated obligations under the 1948 Genocide Convention to punish those who committed acts of genocide, among other items.

“However, the Court found that Myanmar did not directly and publicly incite the commission of genocide by private persons against the Rohingya group in northern Rakhine State,” the ruling states, referring to where the Rohingya lived in Myanmar.

The ICJ ordered the country to immediately cease all ongoing violations, take steps to investigate all persons suspected of committing acts of genocide, ensure that acts of genocide do not continue and adopt measures to bring restitution to the Rohingya. It has given the country two years to report back to the court on these restitution efforts.

The world court stated that Myanmar’s military, police and border guards killed around 10,000 Rohingya civilians in incidents involving mass shootings, sexual violence and arson. These attacks drove more than 810,000 Rohingya out of Rakhine and into Bangladesh as refugees.

ICJ President Yuji Iwasawa said nine judges voted in favor of the ruling and six objected, The Wall Street Journal reported.

The decision comes seven years after Gambia, a largely Muslim country, filed the case. It’s the fourth time that the world court has ruled that a country met the legal threshold to prove genocide since the Nazi Holocaust and the first time that a state has been held responsible, according to Reuters.

Myanmar, which is in the midst of a civil war, has previously denied accusations of genocide.

International law has faced criticism in recent years after South Africa filed its case against Israel, accusing it of committing genocide on Palestinians in Gaza during the nation’s retribution campaign — sparked by a Hamas-led attack on Oct. 7, 2023.

The ICJ ordered Israel in a 13-2 ruling to cease its military operation in May 2024, but Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu vowed to continue until there was “complete victory” over Hamas. Israeli officials have denied South Africa’s accusation of genocide, with the late Sen. Lindsey Graham (R-S.C.) at the time telling the world court to “go to hell” after the ruling.

The world court is limited in how it carries out its orders. Russia ignored a 2022 ruling to stop its invasion of Ukraine, and the U.S. refused the ICJ’s 1986 decision to pay Nicaragua war reparations after the ICJ ruled that the U.S. violated international law.

data.title: Anthropic opens at $111.50 per share after largest IPO ever
data.description:
Artificial intelligence giant Anthropic opened at $111.50 per share on Wednesday, after the company wrapped up the largest initial public offering (IPO) on record.

Anthropic, which is trading under the ticket “ANT,” and certain stockholders sold 980 million shares of the company’s stock valued at $83 per share, the AI firm announced Wednesday. 

That brought the company’s IPO to more than $81.3 billion, the largest in history. Anthropic had aimed to raise more than $64 billion at a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion for its IPO, based on the company’s most recent filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

The Claude maker is the first frontier AI lab to go public, beating competitors such as OpenAI less than six years after co-founders Dario Amodei and Daniela Amodei departed the latter company and founded Anthropic.

Anthropic’s stock dipped below $100 per share within 30 minutes of its Nasdaq Composite debut and was trading at roughly $96.60 per share as of the early afternoon.

Elon Musk’s SpaceX set the previous IPO record in June, raising $75 billion as it went public at $150 per share. The firm, whose stock market debut made Musk the world’s first trillionaire, sold an additional $11 billion worth of shares after its underwriters exercised their option to purchase the maximum amount of shares.

SpaceX’s stock has fluctuated over the last five months and is trading at below $138 per share as of Thursday afternoon.

Anthropic going public coincides with a rocky couple of weeks for the AI industry, as Jensen Huang’s departure from Nvidia sent shockwaves through the company responsible for powering the technology via its chips.

Lawmakers on Capitol Hill have also sounded the alarm bells about Anthropic’s IPO, as Americans express concerns about AI’s impact on the labor market and its implications for humanity.

“The pressure to deliver profits will be immediate, and it will be immense,” Rep. Pat Ryan (D-N.Y.) wrote Wednesday on the social platform X, referring to Anthropic.

“I’m not writing this because I doubt the technology is powerful,” he added. “I’m writing this because I’m terrified of the choices Anthropic will make to justify their valuation.”

data.title: Watch live: Slotkin, Kelly mark one year since 'illegal orders' video sparked Trump backlash
data.description:
Sens. Elissa Slotkin (D-Mich.) and Mark Kelly (D-Ariz.) will speak with reporters Thursday, marking one year since they joined four other Democratic lawmakers in releasing a video reminding military service members they can refuse unlawful orders.

The video drew fierce backlash from President Trump, who accused the lawmakers of sedition and called for their prosecution.

The anniversary comes just weeks after Democrats scored major victories in the midterm elections, setting the stage for renewed clashes with the Trump administration as the party prepares to take control of Congress in January.

The event is scheduled to begin at 2 p.m. EST.

Watch live above.

data.title: Sasse to release memoir on his life, family amid cancer battle
data.description:
Former Sen. Ben Sasse (R-Neb.) announced Thursday he will release a new memoir reflecting on his life and the passage of time next year, which he penned alongside his daughter amid his battle with Stage 4 pancreatic cancer.

“Fighting cancer is… uh…not as fun as you might expect, but…working on a book with your kid is pretty great. Over the past few months, my daughter Alex and I wrote a book in hospital hallways,” Sasse wrote on social platform X. “It’s not a cancer memoir (woof that’s boring) — but some of our reflections on time, habits, workaholism, and family.”

The book, “Redeem the Time: The Strange Gift of Dying and the Lost Art of Living,” is set to be published in March. The former senator’s announcement came almost a year after he was diagnosed with cancer and told he had just months to live.

“We’re all on the clock, and although death is absolutely wicked, the strange ‘gift of dying‘ is that it shatters our self-delusions about control,” he added.

Sasse has been public about his cancer battle, opening up to The New York Times about his diagnosis in an interview earlier this year. During the conversation, published in April, he praised his doctors at MD Anderson Cancer Center in Houston and said, despite his cancer having spread, he felt less pain than he did before. 

At the time, the former lawmaker told the Times the idea of leaving behind his kids was taking a toll on him.

“I didn’t like the idea of my 14-year-old son not having a dad around at 16,” Sasse said in the interview. “I didn’t like the idea of my daughters, who are 22 and 24, not having their dad there to walk them down the aisle. I felt a real heaviness about that.”

In a phone interview with Axios Thursday, Sasse credited his daughter Alex with half of the idea for the book.

“[She] pushed me to do this as a joint project with her. So that was half of it,” Sasse told Axios. “The other half is I’m not dead yet. So why not try to do something to be of use and love to your neighbor and try to serve somebody?””

The former Nebraska senator left the upper chamber in 2023 to become president of the University of Florida, but he resigned the following year after his wife, Melissa, was diagnosed with epilepsy.

In the Axios interview, Sasse said the concept of being rich with time was a central theme of the book.

“We’re not just the materially richest people at any time and place in history, but we’re also the time-richest people,” Sasse told Axios. “And yet, we seem pretty dang miserable. Which is weird, because we ought to be able to make conscious choices about how to invest or redeem the time.”

data.title: Peltola says Alaska voters did not elect her to be partisan
data.description:
Sen.-elect Mary Peltola (D-Alaska) sent a signal Wednesday that she won’t be a partisan Democrat as a member of the Senate, saying voters did not elect her for partisanship.

Peltola told The Associated Press on Wednesday Alaskan voters were straightforward with a message of wanting help with “crippling” fuel, healthcare and necessities prices and that the voters’ support did not come because of a desire for partisanship from the senator-elect.

The Hill’s partners at Decision Desk HQ projected late Tuesday that Peltola, 53, would winthe Alaska Senate race over incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan (R-Alaska).

Peltola’s win means Democrats have netted a total of nine Senate seats, createing a 56-seat majority in the Senate fo rthe party.

Peltola is a former congresswoman from Alaska, and will be the first native-born Alaskan to serve in the U.S. Senate.

The Alaska Democrat’s victory was an upset in a state that commonly leans toward the GOP. But Republicans faced an uphill battle in this year’s midterms, with issues like the unpopular war in Iran, President Trump’s slumping approval rating and concerns about the cost of living weighing the party down.

Sullivan and the GOP have also complained about the existence of a second Dan Sullivan in the race who ran as an indendent. Peltola has denied reporting that her campaign was involved with the second Sullivan running for the Senate.

“As a lifelong Alaskan who has dedicated my career to serving our state, there is no greater honor than having Alaskans’ support in our fight to take on corporate greed, lower costs, and put Alaska first,” Peltola said in a post on the social platform X late Tuesday.

“Thank you, Alaska. Let’s get to work,” she added.

The nine Senate seats that Democrats have flipped is the most in nearly seven decades. The last time Democrats notched nine or more Senate seats in a midterm  former President Dwight Eisenhower was in the White House, per the AP.

data.title: 5 takeaways on Trump's unprecedented summit with Putin, Xi
data.description:
President Trump wrapped a whirlwind three-day trip to Asia on Thursday with an unprecedented trilateral meeting with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin.

The president struck trade deals with the Philippines and Thailand during the Association of Southeast Asian Nations Summit in Manila earlier in the week. 

But the highest-profile stop on Trump’s Asia tour was in Shenzhen, China, where he met with Xi and Putin both one-on-one and then together. 

Democrats hammered Trump for the public coziness with America’s rivals, but the president argued the “old school” of diplomacy hasn’t been working. 

Here are five takeaways from Trump’s trip to Asia.

U.S., Russia, China agree to dialogue on nuclear nonproliferation

As part of a four-point “declaration toward peace” released after Thursday’s summit, Trump, Putin and Xi agreed to participate in an ongoing dialogue on nuclear nonproliferation. 

“The three heads of state reaffirmed that a nuclear war cannot be won and must never be fought. The three countries will conduct a dialogue on reducing nuclear risks and preventing the proliferation of nuclear weapons,” the three leaders said in the joint statement. 

The U.S., China, and Russia are the world’s largest nuclear powers.

“It’s not an easy thing to do, give them up,” Trump said of nuclear arms, seated across from Putin and Xi. “But it’s also vital that we cooperate to combat the threat of nuclear proliferation in other countries around the world. That’s what we’re doing in Iran.”

Observers and U.S. officials had low expectations that any major breakthroughs would be reached with China due to the country’s past resistance to checks on nuclear arms build-up. 

“We do not expect to get to any kind of agreement,” a senior U.S. official told reporters last week, referring to the meeting as “an entry point.” 

China is a member of the Treaty on the Non-Proliferation of Nuclear Weapons, but the Pentagon has estimated the country will likely have more than 1,000 operational nuclear warheads by 2030.

Shots fired at International Criminal Court 

The three countries used the joint declaration to levy criticism against the International Criminal Court, calling on the body to not “abuse” its jurisdiction. 

“The three heads of state recognized that the principle of state consent and respect for immunities of State officials are of paramount importance, and concurred that the International Criminal Court and other similar bodies must not abuse their jurisdiction,” the leaders said in the declaration.

In 2023, the ICC issued an arrest warrant for Putin over alleged war crimes related to the deportation of Ukrainian children as a part of Russia’s war in Ukraine. 

The Trump administration has been an outspoken opponent of the ICC, largely over its prosecution of Israeli leaders over alleged war crimes in Gaza. 

Earlier this year, Secretary of State Marco Rubio pledged that the U.S. would dismantle the international body “brick by brick.” 

While Russia voted in favor of the Rome Statute establishing the court in 1998, China and the U.S. voted against it. 

Trump cozies up to Putin as Ukraine war rages on 

Trump discussed Russia’s ongoing war in Ukraine with Putin and Xi during their meetings on Thursday, saying that his Russian counterpart would like to see the war ended. 

“We are going to be discussing the war between Russia and Ukraine, and we already have. 

President Putin and I have had a long discussion today for quite a while, that’s what pretty pretty much what the discussion was about, and I think things are happening,” Trump said during his trilateral meeting with Putin and Xi.

Trump went on to refer to Ukraine as “the other side” in his remarks. 

“I think that [Putin], and I hope the other side, would like to see an end to that war,” Trump said. 

Trump was outwardly warm toward Putin during their meetings, referring to his Russian counterpart as “his friend” in their first meeting since their summit in Alaska last year. 

“Who is he? He’s my friend.” Trump said walking into the room to greet Putin on Thursday. 

Russia’s war in Ukraine is in its fifth year, but was not mentioned in the joint declaration between the three countries. 

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said on Wednesday that Xi and Trump could pressure Putin into ending the war. 

“If China and the United States will put sanctions, or will say that they will put sanctions, stop export-import trade between Russia and these countries, that’s the end of the war,” Zelensky said in an interview with NBC News. 

Trump reaches trade agreements with Philippines, Thailand 

Prior to traveling to China, Trump announced two separate trade agreements with Thailand and the Philippines during the ASEAN summit in Manila. 

Trump touted what he said was a “landmark” deal with the Philippines on Wednesday, saying it would be great for farmers and those in the energy business. 

Trump praised the deal during a state lunch with the country’s president Ferdinand Marcos Jr. 

“It’s a fair deal for both countries and we’re very happy with that and we didn’t know that that 

was going to take place, but it took place very quickly,” Trump said. 

On Tuesday, Trump announced that as apart of a trade deal with the U.S., Thailand would slash all tariffs on U.S. exports and remove substantial nontariff barriers on various products. 

Trump also noted that Thailand will purchase $2.6 billion in additional U.S. agricultural products, and the deal will be finalized in the coming weeks.

“We’ve been working on this deal for a long time,” the president said. 

Trump to hold press conference on Friday

In a Truth Social post on Thursday, the president said he would discuss both trade deals — and the rest of the trip — during a news conference at the White House on Friday. 

Trump did not hold a press conference in Asia, as is typical of U.S. presidents at the end of high-profile trips abroad. 

He did give an interview to NBC News’s Gabe Gutierrez on the flight back home. 

“I think it was a 12. On a scale of zero to 10, I think it was a 12. It went great, “ Trump said of the trip. “Fantastic relationships built.”

He also said he and Xi talked about artificial intelligence guardrails during their meeting. 

Media coverage of the summit was tightly controlled. 

China barred a Bloomberg reporter from covering the trilateral meeting between the three leaders after the reporter shouted a question during Xi’s bilateral with Trump.

Bloomberg reporter Annmarie Hordern had asked Trump during his bilateral with Xi if former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has been disloyal to the U.S. Trump did not respond to the question. 

Trump lightly criticized other press restrictions during the trip earlier on Thursday. 

“It’s too bad the media couldn’t see some of it, because every move was perfectly executed,” Trump said, referring to the summit.

data.title: Chuck Todd says Democrats should 'start with tariffs' to lower cost of living
data.description:
Former “Meet the Press” moderator and political pundit Chuck Todd said he expects the new, Democrat-led Congress to focus on lowering living costs, beginning with walking back the second Trump administration’s sweeping tariffs on foreign goods.

“In the first hundred days, it’s about going after things this administration has done to raise the cost on the American public,” Todd told anchor Leland Vittert of NewsNation, The Hill’s sister network. “You start with tariffs. It’s sitting right there.”

“The Iran war is probably number two on the agenda in that its impact on people’s bottom line,” Todd added.

Democrats took back both chambers of Congress in a sweeping “blue wave” during November’s midterms, flipping GOP-held seats in key battlegrounds including Texas, Kansas, Maine and South Carolina on Election Day — and, more recently, in Mississippi and Alaska.

Prior to the elections, voters cited rising costs and the war in Iran under the first half of Presiednt Trump’s second term as top concerns impacting their choices at the polls. In a Reuters/Ipsos survey released the night before Election Day, 48 percent of respondents ranked affordability as the most important factor in deciding their vote.

In a Gallup survey, conducted last month, nearly half of those polled marked the economy as an “extremely important” factor in casting their ballots. In the same poll, 47 percent said the same of the Iran war, while an additional 30 percent called the conflict “very important” to their election decisions.

Following the midterms, some Republicans admitted the Iran war and its associated economic impacts set the stage for the huge GOP losses, though the president has defended the conflict, instead blaming the blowout on candidate quality.

Texas Sen. Ted Cruz (R) pointed to cost of living as a “top issue” for voters, saying, “Food is too high. Gas is too high. Diesel is too high. Insurance is too high. Life is too high.”

“Tariffs have made everything too expensive, and the Iran war has dragged on too long,” Cruz added.

Vice President Vance also placed the blame for GOP’s losses on the Iran war, saying, “The reason we lost is the war.”

“If you’d like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay. Agree or disagree, that’s at least honest,” Vance said.

During his interview with Leeland, Todd also warned Democrats to focus less on “retribution” against the executive branch and more on “operating the entire time in making government easier on people’s lives” — calls which came as the party tees up sweeping investigations into Trump administration officials.

“There are more effective ways to accomplish the larger goal of accountability on the executive branch, and at the same time, bringing down the cost for the American people,” he said.

data.title: No enemy required: Are all our systems really just this unreliable?
data.description:
In the span of five days, Americans lost access to some of the systems they depend on most. Microsoft 365 suffered an outage that disrupted email and collaboration tools for about a day. The Federal Aviation Administration halted departures nationwide after equipment on its telecommunications network became unstable. Three days later, Chase banking customers found themselves unable to move their own money.

So far, none of these events has been attributed to a cyberattack. Microsoft says it found no sign of one. Chase says its trouble was not cyber-related. The FAA says the evidence shows no indication of a cyberattack, and names a remote radio site where a contractor had been working as one of two potential sources while its investigation continues. Federal officials say they see no evidence that the outages are connected or that an adversary was behind them.

That should concern us far more than it seems to.

Over the last two decades, organizations have poured money into protecting their systems from hostile actors. We have built entire industries around cybersecurity. We run penetration tests, monitor hostile traffic, buy threat intelligence and employ teams whose sole purpose is keeping adversaries outside the perimeter. Those investments matter as the threats from the outside are real.

But by the organizations’ own accounts, at least two of these disruptions did not start outside the fence. They began during planned technical work. The danger may not have been a sophisticated attacker — it may have been merely a routine upgrade.

I spent 23 years in FAA air traffic control and retired as an air traffic manager. Since 2006, I have practiced and taught the FAA’s safety risk management process. I have watched organizations succeed because changes were evaluated before they went live. I have also watched them struggle when responsibility for a change became diffused and nobody owned the outcome.

Consider what has been disclosed. The FAA says a contractor had been working at a remote communications site, including deploying a new router, and that the site is one of two potential sources of the trouble. The root cause remains under investigation.

Microsoft said an earlier network capacity upgrade caused trouble after a later system change, and its preliminary post-incident report describes a latent defect that left servers overwhelmed under load. By the company’s own account, planned work exposed a hidden flaw. It was not an attack.

Chase has attributed its outage to a software bug and has not said how the bug reached its systems.

That makes two of three incidents tied to planned work by their owners’ own accounts. I won’t speculate on the third.

A firewall can block hostile traffic. An intrusion detection system can flag suspicious activity. A security operations center can watch for adversaries around the clock. But none of those controls asks whether maintenance should happen in the middle of a Friday. None asks whether a rollback plan exists, whether a dependency was overlooked, or whether the people approving a change understand what happens if it fails. Those questions belong to management, not technology.

Aviation learned that lesson long ago. The agency’s latest safety management order took effect in September. Its requirement is plain: A planned change cannot proceed without a risk acceptance signature from a management official, and the decision is recorded in the agency’s risk register. Federal bank examiners have guidance of their own — a handbook that calls for a formal process for controlling and approving changes.

On paper, the process is simple, but a procedure on paper is not accountability in practice. The FAA has described the Nov. 13 router replacement as routine work of a kind done for decades without impact. I understand why. In my experience, though, “routine” might be the most dangerous word in any operation. Novel changes get scrutiny because everybody sees the risk. Routine changes get a nod because they worked the last hundred times. The hundred-and-first is the one that makes the front page of the newspapers.

I don’t know whether the router replacement was handled as a planned change under the FAA’s orders; the agency hasn’t said. The Washington Post reported on Nov. 17, citing a person close to the investigation, that an FAA official supervised the work, tested it and signed off shortly before the ground stop. If so, a signature exists. I still don’t know whether anyone accepted the risk before the work began, what assessment supported that decision or what testing was done against the live network. As members of Congress promise oversight on the ground stop, those are the questions to put to the FAA.

The same ones should be put to Microsoft and Chase: What changed? Who approved it? What testing did it pass before it touched a live system?

Those aren’t technical questions. They are leadership questions. Microsoft has released a preliminary post-incident report to its customers. The FAA and Chase should do the same, and all three should answer in language that customers, passengers and regulators can all understand.

More money will not fix this by itself. Neither will a new vendor, a new platform or a taller firewall. The next major disruption may not require an enemy at all. It may require nothing more than a work order and nobody clearly accountable for the result.

Vincent E. Bianco III is principal consultant of Marivin Consulting Services LLC and spent 23 years in FAA air traffic control, retiring as an air traffic manager.
